Yes -- in the sense that the quoted number is not the
impedance of the oscillating circuit.  It is the impedance
linearised about a point at which the circuit does not stay.

Let the internal nodes be $A,B,C$.  The (unstable) d-c solution is

$$
A=B=C=V_M\approx V_{DD}/2 ,
$$

with every device saturated with the $g_{mn},g_{mp}$ used above.
For a symmetric supply perturbation the symmetry gives
$\delta A=\delta B=\delta C$, so for every stage incrementally
$\delta v_{in}=\delta v_{out}$: the stage momentarily looks like a
PMOS diode in series with an NMOS diode between $V_{DD}$ and ground.
Three such stages in parallel give

$$
R_X \approx \frac13\Bigl(\frac1{g_{mn}}+\frac1{g_{mp}}\Bigr).
$$

That operating point has loop gain $>1$ and is unstable.  In
oscillation $A,B,C$ are large, roughly rail-to-rail waveforms shifted
by $T_{osc}/3$; in particular $v_{in}\ne v_{out}$ for a stage except at
the brief crossing instants.  There is no fixed $Q$ point about which
to linearise:

* $g_{mn}$ and $g_{mp}$ are not constants; over a period each device
goes through cut-off, triode and saturation.
* In a non-switching inverter one device is essentially off, so there
is no diode-connected d-c path from $V_{DD}$ to ground.
* The supply current is not a static crowbar current; it consists
mainly of pulses charging the node capacitances.  Only the stage
actually switching draws appreciable through-current, and only
briefly.

Hence there is no time-invariant small-signal $R_X$ of the quoted
form; the incremental supply conductance is periodic in time,
depending on the phase of the oscillation at which the perturbation
is applied, with mixing to $f_{test}\pm nf_{osc}$.

A slow, period-averaged measurement gives instead

$$
\bar I_{DD}\approx 3C_L V_{DD} f_{osc}(V_{DD}),\qquad
R_{X,\text{avg}}=\left(\frac{d\bar I_{DD}}{dV_{DD}}\right)^{-1}
 =\frac{1}{3C_L\!\left[f_{osc}+V_{DD}\,df_{osc}/dV_{DD}\right]},
$$

which is in general quite different from
$\tfrac13\bigl(1/g_{mn}+1/g_{mp}\bigr)$ evaluated at the metastable
point.

The expression  

  RX ≈ (1/3) (1/gmn + 1/gmp)  

is valid only for the special situation that was implicitly assumed in the original
derivation: every inverter is sitting at the same, fixed bias point (normally VDD/2) so
that both its NMOS and PMOS are simultaneously conducting.  
Then:

• each stage looks like two diode-connected devices in series,  
• the three stages are in parallel with respect to the supply node, so their
  resistances add in parallel, giving the extra 1/3 factor.

That bias condition exists when the ring is at rest or at the very first
infinitesimal start-up of the oscillation; once a large-signal oscillation is
established the operating point is no longer static:

1. At any instant only one stage (the one that is changing state) is near its
   switching threshold; the other two outputs are close to the rails.
2. In the two “quiet” stages one of the transistors is completely off
   (gm ≈ 0), so the path from VDD to ground through that stage is open and the
   stage contributes essentially no conductance to the supply node.
3. The stage that is switching still looks like two diode-connected devices, so
   while it is switching the instantaneous resistance seen from the supply node
   is  
  Rinst ≈ 1/gmn + 1/gmp.  
   (The factor 1/3 is gone because only one stage is contributing.)
4. During the large portion of the period in which no stage is switching,
   RX(t) is practically infinite.

Hence RX becomes a periodic, time-varying quantity:  
 • most of the time it is very large (≈ ∞),  
 • for short intervals it drops to ≈ 1/gmn + 1/gmp.

The average (or any effective) value is therefore much larger than the constant
value obtained for the non-oscillating case, and the simple expression with the
1/3 factor is no longer applicable once the ring is oscillating.

          RX ≈ (1/3)(1/gmn + 1/gmp)

assumes a dc operating point at which every inverter is biased right at its
switching threshold (≈ VDD / 2).  
At that bias both the NMOS and the PMOS of every cell are ON, so each cell
looks like two diode-connected transistors in series and the small-signal
resistance of one inverter is  

          rINV = 1/gmn + 1/gmp .

Because the three inverters are fed from the same supply node, those three
resistances are in parallel, giving the factor 1/3.

Once the loop is actually oscillating that bias point no longer exists.  
At any instant an inverter’s output is either near 0 V or near VDD (except for
the short switching interval).  Therefore, for most of the period

• when the output is low, the PMOS is ON and the NMOS is OFF → small-signal
  resistance ≈ 1/gmp ;

• when the output is high, the NMOS is ON and the PMOS is OFF → small-signal
  resistance ≈ 1/gmn .

Only for a brief moment, while an inverter is crossing mid-rail, are both
devices simultaneously on and the “two-devices-in-series” model valid.

Hence the instantaneous resistance seen at the supply node is now

          RX(t) ≈ 1/[ gON,1(t) + gON,2(t) + gON,3(t) ] ,

where gON,i(t) is the gm of the single device that happens to be ON in the i-th
stage at that time.  For identical stages this swings between

          RX ≈ 1/(3 gmn)   (all three outputs high)   and
          RX ≈ 1/(3 gmp)   (all three outputs low),

with short excursions to the earlier value (1/3)(1/gmn + 1/gmp) during the
switching instants.

So the original number is correct only for the small-signal, non-oscillating
(or “start-up”) condition.  In steady-state oscillation the looking-in
resistance is lower, time-varying, and is roughly 1/(3 gmON) rather than
(1/3)(1/gmn + 1/gmp).

## Short answer

**No – the expression does not change.** $R_X=\tfrac{1}{3}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{g_{mn}}+\tfrac{1}{g_{mp}}\right)$ is a *local, instantaneous* (linearized) result, and the same derivation is valid at every instant of the oscillation. What changes is only that $g_{mn}$ and $g_{mp}$ – and therefore $R_X$ – are no longer constants but functions of time.

## Why the formula is unaffected by oscillation

The small‑signal resistance seen at a node is the local slope $dI/dV$ at the *instantaneous* bias point. It depends on (i) the instantaneous transconductances and (ii) the topology, i.e. on which nodes carry small‑signal current. Both of these are unchanged by the fact that the loop is oscillating.

It is worth seeing exactly what the "two diode‑connected devices in series" picture is really using, because that is the part a student might fear breaks down. For one inverter, with $v$ the small‑signal supply voltage, $a_{in}$ the gate voltage and $a_{out}$ the drain voltage, and with $r_o$ and gate current neglected:

- PMOS (source $=v$, gate $=a_{in}$): $i_{d,p}=g_{mp}(a_{in}-v)$
- NMOS (source $=0$, gate $=a_{in}$): $i_{d,n}=g_{mn}\,a_{in}$
- KCL at the drain node (the only other connection is a gate, i.e. **zero current**):
  $g_{mp}(a_{in}-v)+g_{mn}\,a_{in}=0 \;\Rightarrow\; a_{in}=v\,\dfrac{g_{mp}}{g_{mp}+g_{mn}}$

The current into the supply node is $i=g_{mp}(v-a_{in})=\dfrac{g_{mp}g_{mn}}{g_{mp}+g_{mn}}\,v$, so

$$R_{\text{one}}=\frac{v}{i}=\frac{1}{g_{mp}}+\frac{1}{g_{mn}}$$

Note the crucial assumption is **not** "the input is at AC ground" (that would give only $1/g_{mp}$) and **not** "gate is literally tied to drain." It is simply *the gate/output nodes carry no small‑signal current*. In the ring those nodes connect only to the gates of the neighbouring inverters, so they carry no resistive current whether the circuit is in a (hypothetical) DC state or swinging in steady‑state oscillation. Hence the same $R_{\text{one}}$ holds at every instant, and the three identical branches in parallel at the supply rail give exactly $\tfrac{1}{3}R_{\text{one}}$. (In the symmetric ring the floating nodes all land at the same potential anyway, so the literal "diode‑connected" picture is consistent too.)

## What *does* change (the caveats worth stating)

1. **There is no DC operating point.** An odd number of inverting stages has no stable DC equilibrium, so the original "DC number" was really evaluated around an *assumed* bias. The formula is just the slope at whatever bias you freeze.
2. **The value becomes time‑varying.** During oscillation the bias of each inverter moves around the cycle, so $g_{mn}(t),g_{mp}(t)$ move, and $R_X(t)$ follows the same formula but is no longer constant. When an inverter's input is near a rail, one device is off ($g_m\to0$), that branch's resistance $\to\infty$, and $R_X$ is large for that phase.
3. **A single number requires an averaging convention.** If you need one value (e.g. for supply design), a time average is not the same as evaluating the formula at the mid‑rail bias, because $1/g_m$ is a nonlinear function of the bias current.
4. **Frozen‑bias $R_X$ ≠ impedance at $f_{osc}$.** The linearized resistance above is the instantaneous derivative. The actual incremental impedance *at the oscillation frequency* of the periodically time‑varying (nonlinear) circuit can differ; that is a different quantity and is not what the $g_m$‑based expression represents.

## Bottom line

The symbolic answer and its derivation are unchanged by oscillation – the small‑signal resistance is a local property of the operating point, and oscillation does not alter the local model. The only difference is that, because the operating point now travels around the cycle, $g_{mn},g_{mp}$ and hence $R_X$ are time‑dependent rather than fixed. So: *same formula, time‑varying value.*

**Why the formula is correct at DC.** Look at what is really tied to the supply node: the three PMOS *sources*. The PMOS *gates* are the previous stage's outputs and the PMOS *drains* are each stage's own output – so, in general, the gates are **not** tied to the drains. The "two diode‑connected devices in series" picture is therefore not a topological fact; it is true only when, for the small‑signal signal of interest, the inverter's input node equals its output node (gate small‑signal = drain small‑signal). At the symmetric bias point $V_{DD}/2$, and for a DC/low‑frequency perturbation at the supply pin, the linearized ring forces *all* node perturbations to be equal, so each transistor does come out diode‑connected. Then each inverter branch is $1/g_{mp}$ (PMOS) in series with $1/g_{mn}$ (NMOS), and the three branches in parallel give $R_X=(1/3)(1/g_{mn}+1/g_{mp})$. That is a perfectly good **DC** number.

**Why it changes when oscillating.** Oscillation is a finite‑frequency phenomenon, and at the oscillation frequency the inverter's input is *not* at the same AC potential as its output – they are phase‑shifted (by $120^\circ$ per stage in the ideal 3‑stage case, by the inverter's actual phase at $\omega_0$ in general). Hence, for the oscillating component, gate $\neq$ drain: the devices are **not** diode‑connected at $\omega_0$, and the series‑resistor model of each inverter falls apart. Doing the small‑signal KCL at $\omega_0$ (with the node capacitances that set $\omega_0$) shows that the three output phasors are no longer equal, and the impedance looking into the supply node becomes a *complex, frequency‑dependent* quantity whose real part at $\omega_0$ is generally different from the real DC value $(1/3)(1/g_{mn}+1/g_{mp})$. In other words, the diode shortcut evaluates the wrong (zero‑frequency) point of the supply‑node impedance; the impedance that the oscillator actually loads the supply with, at the oscillation frequency, is not that simple sum. (As a side note, an oscillating circuit's small‑signal model is periodically time‑varying, so it doesn't even have a single time‑invariant "resistance" at the supply pin.)

**Caveat / what *doesn't* change.** If by "small‑signal resistance" one means strictly the zero‑frequency Thévenin resistance of the circuit *linearized and frozen at the symmetric operating point*, then that particular mathematical object is of course untouched by the large‑signal oscillation. But that is not the impedance relevant to the oscillation, and it is exactly the value the diode‑connected reasoning was meant to capture. So the practical answer to "does the answer change if the circuit oscillates?" is **yes**: the formula is the DC/low‑frequency value at the symmetric bias point, and the supply‑node impedance seen during oscillation (at $\omega_0$) is different because the inverter inputs and outputs are out of phase and the transistors are no longer diode‑connected.

**Short answer: yes – once the ring actually oscillates, (1/3)(1/gmn + 1/gmp) no longer describes what the supply node sees.** That expression is the linearization about the *metastable* DC operating point (all six transistors saturated, every node at the trip voltage, Vin = Vout for each inverter). Oscillation means the circuit has left that point, and the resistance seen from the supply node in the oscillating state is a completely different, time‑varying, and much larger quantity.

**Where the formula comes from (and why it is "right" only at the metastable point).**
At the metastable equilibrium, injecting a test voltage vx at the supply node forces, by KCL at each output node (gates draw no DC current), all internal node increments to the same value v = vx·gmp/(gmn+gmp). Hence every gate and drain of every transistor move together incrementally, i.e. each device indeed looks diode‑connected, each inverter presents 1/gmn + 1/gmp from supply to ground, and the three in parallel give RX = (1/3)(1/gmn + 1/gmp). Note that this linearized result already includes the feedback loop (the loop does not modify it at DC); so the formula is exactly the small‑signal resistance *of the metastable bias point*.

**But that bias point is unstable.** A loop of three inverting gain stages with |gain| > 1 per stage has right‑half‑plane poles; any noise kicks the circuit off the metastable point and it settles into rail‑to‑rail oscillation. So "the circuit oscillates" and "the circuit sits at the point where each inverter looks like two diode‑connected devices" are mutually exclusive statements.

**What the supply node sees during oscillation.**
- Most of the time each inverter's input is near a rail. If the input is high, that inverter's PMOS is off: the supply path through it is blocked. If the input is low, the PMOS is on but carries no DC current (the NMOS is off), so the inverter again presents a very high incremental resistance (off‑device/ro‑scale).
- Only during the brief switching instants are both devices conducting (shoot‑through), and only then does the inverter momentarily resemble the diode‑connected pair.
- Consequently RX(t) is a strongly time‑varying periodic quantity: very large for most of the cycle, dipping toward (1/gmn+1/gmp) only for a small fraction of it. The effective DC resistance seen from the supply is VDD/Iavg, where Iavg is just the switching/shoot‑through current (≈ C·VDD·fosc per stage) – typically tens to hundreds of kΩ, versus the ~kΩ/3 the formula predicts.
- More fundamentally, linearizing about a *periodic* steady state yields a linear periodically time‑varying network: a small test tone at f produces responses at f ± k·fosc, so a single number "RX" is not even well defined there (one needs a conversion matrix/describing function).

**Conclusion.** The expression RX ≈ (1/3)(1/gmn + 1/gmp) is valid only for the unstable equilibrium (or if oscillation were somehow suppressed). If the circuit oscillates, the premise "each inverter is two diode‑connected devices in series" collapses because the transistors are hard‑switched between cutoff and deep triode; the resistance seen looking into the supply node becomes time‑varying and orders of magnitude larger. So yes, the answer changes.

Only at that point does each transistor's gate small‑signal voltage equal its own drain voltage, so each device mimics a diode‑connected transistor, and each inverter looks like $1/g_{mp} + 1/g_{mn}$ from $V_{DD}$ to ground, with three such paths in parallel.

**But that bias point is exactly the unstable equilibrium.** The oscillation condition (loop gain $\geq 1$ with the three stages supplying 180° of phase shift plus the 180° of inversion) means the linearized loop has right‑half‑plane poles *about that same point*. So "the circuit oscillates" and "the circuit sits at the bias point used to derive $R_X$" are mutually exclusive: any perturbation grows until the nodes swing rail‑to‑rail, and the diode‑connected picture ($v_g = v_d$, devices in saturation) is destroyed.

**What the supply node actually sees during oscillation.** The inverters now act as switches, so the resistance looking into the supply node is a *time‑varying, large‑signal* quantity:

- In the quasi‑static states (output high or low), one transistor of each inverter is cut off: there is no DC path from the supply node to ground at all, so the instantaneous resistance is essentially infinite (only capacitive charging current flows).
- During the brief transitions, both devices of a switching inverter are on, presenting a low triode‑region path $\approx r_{on,p} + r_{on,n}$, much smaller than $1/g_{mn} + 1/g_{mp}$.
- The meaningful (averaged) resistance is therefore $R_{eff} \approx V_{DD}/I_{avg}$, with $I_{avg} \approx 3 f_{osc} C_L V_{DD} + I_{shoot\text{-}through}$ set by the switching frequency, load capacitances and overlap current — none of which appear in $\tfrac{1}{3}(1/g_{mn}+1/g_{mp})$.

**A deeper point.** Small‑signal resistance is defined by linearizing about a *steady* operating point. With RHP poles present, a test current injected at the supply node does not produce a settled proportional voltage; the response grows into the limit cycle. So during oscillation there is no LTI small‑signal $R_X$ at all — only a periodically time‑varying impedance (with frequency conversion) and its large‑signal average.

**Conclusion.** The expression $\tfrac{1}{3}(1/g_{mn}+1/g_{mp})$ is valid only for the (unstable) metastable DC equilibrium — i.e., for the linearized circuit *before* oscillation starts, or if oscillation is prevented (loop broken, gain per stage < 2). If the circuit truly oscillates, the answer changes: the supply sees a switched, time‑varying load whose effective resistance is governed by the large‑signal switching dynamics ($\approx V_{DD}/I_{avg}$), not by the diode‑connected $1/g_m$ values.

**What the calculation actually assumes.** The expression $R_X \approx \frac{1}{3}(1/g_{mn} + 1/g_{mp})$ is the linearization about the *metastable DC equilibrium* of the loop, i.e. the point where every inverter sits at $V_{in} = V_{out} \approx V_{DD}/2$ with all six transistors in saturation. At that point a test signal on the supply rail forces every node in the loop to move by the same amount (the loop equations admit only the symmetric solution), so each transistor sees $v_{gs} = v_{ds}$ (NMOS) and $v_{sg} = v_{sd}$ (PMOS) – hence the "diode‑connected pair in series" per inverter, and three such branches in parallel from the supply node to ground. Nothing wrong with that algebra – *at that bias point*.

**Why oscillation invalidates it.** That equilibrium is unstable; its instability *is* the oscillation. A circuit that oscillates never resides at $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_{DD}/2$, so the $g_m$'s used in the formula are not the transconductances the devices actually exhibit. In the periodic steady state:

- **Most of the cycle:** each inverter has one device cut off (outputs sit near the rails), so there is *no conducting path at all* from the supply node to ground. The instantaneous resistance seen at the supply node is essentially open‑circuit; the supply only delivers capacitive charging current.
- **During the brief switching overlaps:** exactly one inverter has both devices on, giving a path of roughly $1/g_{mn} + 1/g_{mp}$ – through *one* inverter, not three in parallel.
- **Cycle‑averaged (incremental) resistance:** the average supply current is the dynamic current $I_{avg} \approx 3 C_L V_{DD} f_{osc}$ (plus short‑circuit current), so the effective resistance is $dV_{DD}/dI_{avg}$, typically kilo‑ohms – an order of magnitude or more larger than $\frac{1}{3}(1/g_{mn}+1/g_{mp})$, which is only a few hundred ohms. Formally, linearizing about a periodic orbit yields a periodically time‑varying impedance (with frequency conversion), not a constant $R_X$.

**Conclusion.** The quoted value is correct only for the (unstable) DC solution – physically, at most during the infinitesimal start‑up transient before the swings grow. Once the ring oscillator is oscillating, the resistance seen looking into the supply node becomes a large, time‑varying quantity set by switching behavior and load‑capacitor charging, not by the diode‑connected $1/g_m$ picture. So yes, the answer changes: $R_X \approx \frac{1}{3}(1/g_{mn}+1/g_{mp})$ does not describe the oscillating circuit.

The answer is **yes**, the computed resistance $R_X$ would change (or rather, the model used to compute it is no longer valid) if the circuit is oscillating.

Here is the detailed reasoning:

1.  **Validity of the Initial Calculation:**
    The formula $R_X \approx \frac{1}{3} \left( \frac{1}{g_{mn}} + \frac{1}{g_{mp}} \right)$ is derived using a **small-signal linearized model**.
    *   The factor $1/3$ implies that the three inverters are in parallel as seen from the supply node (Vdd). This is true for DC current flow.
    *   The term $\left( \frac{1}{g_{mn}} + \frac{1}{g_{mp}} \right)$ represents the resistance of a single inverter modeled as two diode-connected transistors in series. This approximation ($r \approx 1/g_m$) is valid only when $V_{gs} \approx V_{ds}$.
    *   This condition ($V_{gs} \approx V_{ds}$) holds true for both NMOS and PMOS transistors only when the inverter input is at the switching threshold (typically $V_{dd}/2$), where both transistors are in the saturation region (or triode region depending on $V_{dd}$) and $V_{gs} \approx V_{ds} \approx V_{dd}/2$.
    *   Thus, the computed $R_X$ represents the **small-signal resistance at the DC bias point**.

2.  **Behavior During Oscillation:**
    *   A ring oscillator relies on the **switching** action of the inverters. The input signal swings rail-to-rail (from 0 to $V_{dd}$).
    *   During the oscillation cycle, the transistors move through different regions:
        *   **Cutoff:** One transistor is off ($g_m \approx 0$).
        *   **Triode/Saturation:** The other transistor is on.
    *   The condition $V_{gs} \approx V_{ds}$ is **not** maintained throughout the cycle. For example, when the input is low ($0V$), the NMOS is off ($V_{gs}=0$) and the PMOS is on ($V_{gs} \approx -V_{dd}$). Here $V_{gs} \neq V_{ds}$.
    *   Consequently, the transconductances $g_{mn}$ and $g_{mp}$ are **not constant**; they vary with $V_{gs}$ and the drain current $I_D$.
    *   The resistance of the branch $1/g_{mn} + 1/g_{mp}$ will vary with time.

3.  **Frequency Effects:**
    *   The initial calculation ignores capacitive effects ($C_{gs}, C_{gd}, C_{db}$).
    *   At the oscillation frequency $\omega_0$, the impedance looking into the supply node will have a reactive (imaginary) component due to these capacitances. The "resistance" (real part) will also be affected by the frequency-dependent impedance of the transistors.

**Conclusion:**
The computed value is a **DC or low-frequency small-signal approximation** valid only at the bias point. If the circuit is oscillating (large-signal steady state), the transistors are switching, the "diode-connected" assumption breaks down, $g_m$ varies, and capacitive effects become significant. Therefore, the small-signal resistance $R_X$ is not constant and is not given by the simple formula.

**Answer:** Yes, the answer changes. The formula is only valid for small signals around the DC bias point. During oscillation, the transistors switch, invalidating the diode-connected model and making the resistance time-varying and frequency-dependent.

    *   There are three inverters connected in parallel to the supply node (the top wire).

    *   The resistance of a diode-connected transistor in saturation is approximately $1/g_m$.
    *   So, the resistance of one inverter branch is $R_{branch} \approx \frac{1}{g_{mn}} + \frac{1}{g_{mp}}$.
    *   Since there are 3 identical branches in parallel, the total resistance is $R_X \approx R_{branch} / 3$.

2.  **The "Diode-Connected" Assumption:**
    The statement "each inverter behaves as two diode-connected devices in series" implies that for each inverter, the drain voltage is approximately equal to the gate voltage ($V_d \approx V_g$).
    *   For a CMOS inverter, $V_{g,n} = V_{g,p} = V_{in}$ and $V_{d,n} = V_{d,p} = V_{out}$.
    *   The condition $V_{out} \approx V_{in}$ occurs when the inverter is biased at the switching threshold, i.e., $V_{in} \approx V_{dd}/2$.
    *   At this point, both transistors are in the saturation region (active region), and the small-signal model consists of the transconductances $g_{mn}$ and $g_{mp}$.

3.  **Behavior During Oscillation:**
    *   In a 3-stage ring oscillator, the inverters are cascaded. The signal at the input of the second inverter is 180° out of phase with the first, and the third is 180° out of phase with the second (or 360°/0° with the first, but delayed).
    *   Actually, for a ring oscillator, the phase shift per stage is 180°. For 3 stages, the total phase shift is 540°, which is equivalent to 180°.
    *   This means the inputs of the three inverters are phase-shifted by 120° ($2\pi/3$) relative to each other.
    *   Consequently, **they cannot all be at the crossover point ($V_{dd}/2$) simultaneously.**
    *   At any given instant:
        *   One inverter might be in the transition region (crossover), where the "diode-connected" model is roughly valid.
        *   The other two inverters will be either in the **Cutoff** region (one transistor off, $g_m \approx 0$) or the **Linear/Triode** region (one transistor on, $V_{ds}$ small).
    *   When a transistor is in Cutoff, the resistance looking into the supply is effectively infinite (open circuit).
    *   When a transistor is in the Linear region, the resistance is low (roughly $1/g_m$ or lower), but it is not the "diode-connected" series resistance.

4.  **Conclusion:**
    The formula assumes a static DC bias where all inverters are active. In an oscillating ring oscillator, the bias point is time-varying. The transistors switch states.
    *   The resistance $R_X$ is **time-varying**.
    *   The static formula $\frac{1}{3} (1/g_{mn} + 1/g_{mp})$ is only valid instantaneously when an inverter is at the crossover point, or as a small-signal approximation around the average bias point.
    *   Since the inverters are not all in the "diode-connected" state at the same time, the parallel combination of 3 such branches does not exist.
    *   Therefore, the specific value computed by "somebody" does not hold for the oscillating circuit as a constant DC resistance. The effective resistance seen by the supply will be different (likely higher on average, as branches turn off).

**Answer:** Yes, the answer changes. The formula assumes all inverters are biased at the midpoint ($V_{dd}/2$), which is impossible in a ring oscillator where inputs are phase-shifted. Thus, the "diode-connected" model is invalid for the whole circuit, and $R_X$ becomes a time-varying quantity, not the constant value given by the formula.

They represent the slope of the I-V curves ($dI/dV$) at that specific bias point.

2.  **Bias Point of a Ring Oscillator:** In a symmetric ring oscillator (like the 3-inverter ring shown), the DC bias point for each inverter is typically at the switching threshold, i.e., $V_{in} = V_{out} \approx V_{DD}/2$. At this point, both the NMOS and PMOS transistors are active (in saturation or triode region), and their transconductances $g_{mn}$ and $g_{mp}$ are determined by the DC supply voltage $V_{DD}$ and the transistor sizing ($W/L$).

3.  **Oscillation vs. Bias:** Oscillation is a **large-signal AC phenomenon**. It is a limit cycle that occurs *around* the DC bias point. The signal swings from $V_{DD}$ to $0$, but the *average* (DC) voltage at the nodes remains $V_{DD}/2$. Since the DC supply $V_{DD}$ is constant (and assuming no supply resistance that causes sag), the DC operating point does not shift.

4.  **Validity of the Model:** The text's model ("each inverter behaves as two diode-connected devices in series") is a small-signal approximation valid around the bias point $V_{DD}/2$. Specifically, when $V_{in} \approx V_{out}$, $V_{gs} \approx V_{ds}$, making the transistors effectively diode-connected. The resistance looking into the relevant node (in this case, the supply node, implying the PMOS sources or a common node) is dominated by $1/g_m$.

5.  **Conclusion:** Since the oscillation is a large-signal effect superimposed on a fixed DC bias point, the transconductances $g_{mn}$ and $g_{mp}$ used in the small-signal calculation remain unchanged. Therefore, the calculated value of $R_X$ remains valid and does not change.

**Note:** While the *small-signal* resistance $R_X$ doesn't change, the *instantaneous* (large-signal) resistance seen by the supply would vary as the transistors switch between on and off states. However, the question asks about the *computed* small-signal resistance, which is a linear parameter fixed by the bias point.

**Answer:** No, the answer does not change. The resistance $R_X$ is a small-signal parameter determined by the DC bias point ($V_{DD}/2$), which is unaffected by the AC oscillation.
